experiment.name: Parasite load in severe vs mild canine babesiosis: synthesis of published contrasts (SV-02a)
experiment.description: Do dogs with severe babesiosis carry a higher parasite load than dogs with mild disease, inside one species and one outcome class? The package hypothesis is that dogs differ more in damage per parasite (tolerance) than in load (resistance); part a asks what the published load-by-outcome contrasts can say.

parameters.pool_rule: REML + Hartung-Knapp only with >= 3 independent units sharing species, outcome class and definition

experiment.summary: No pooled estimate: no species and outcome class has 3 or more independent units with load against outcome (largest cell 2 units; 6 units in 5 cells, 4 species groups). Only one unit gives a load difference by outcome: B. canis nonsurvivors vs survivors (CB516, 8 vs 7 dogs, death includes euthanasia), Hedges g of log load -0.17 (-1.19 to 0.85); 1 of 6 units report significantly higher load with severity (B. canis HES score, rho 0.35). No hypothesis tests (0 of 0).

sections.heading: Question
paragraphs: Do dogs with severe babesiosis carry more parasites than dogs with mild disease, inside one Babesia species and one outcome class? SV-02 asks whether dogs differ more in damage per parasite (tolerance) than in load (resistance); part a looks at what the published load-by-outcome contrasts can say.

sections.heading: What was done
paragraphs: From the SV-G2 extraction (42 independent units with severity rows), every parasite load row was taken: 10 rows. 6 rows in 6 units compare load with a severity or outcome definition. The experimental dose contrast (CB105, CH09) and the rows where load defines the groups were set aside.

The spec allowed a random-effects pool (REML, Hartung-Knapp interval) of the standardised difference in log load only where 3 or more independent units share one species, one outcome class and one definition. Otherwise each unit is shown in a direction table with its load method and sample timing. Effects were computed where the paper prints group n and dispersion.

A separate list collects results of the form 'severe disease at low load' or 'protection at unchanged load': 5 from the SV-G2 rows and 5 from a keyword screen of the appraisal notes (17 notes matched; 5 kept after reading).

sections.heading: Result
paragraphs: No cell reached the pooling rule. The largest cell has 2 units (B. canis severity grade, two different definitions). The primary analysis therefore has no pooled effect: this is a lack of data, not evidence for either hypothesis.

B. canis mortality (CB516, 8 nonsurvivors vs 7 survivors, death includes euthanasia): median load 1.25% vs 1.2%, Hedges g of log load -0.17 (-1.19 to 0.85). With these group sizes only a difference of about 1.6 SD could be detected, so the null is weak.

B. canis haematological score (CB141, ddPCR load): rho 0.35 (0.23 to 0.46, n 222). In the same cohort antibody level correlates more strongly, and in the opposite direction: rho -0.65 (-0.73 to -0.56, n 166). The two intervals do not overlap, but the samples differ and the score is built from blood counts, so this is not a formal comparison.

Large Babesia, jaundiced (late) vs anaemic (early) form (CB220): load slightly lower in the late form; with an assumed equal split of 20 dogs, g -0.39 (-1.27 to 0.49). The more severe form is also the later one, so stage and severity are mixed here (the question of SV-01). B. gibsoni (CB045): load unrelated to pancreatic injury (r 0.09, n 20). Mixed B. gibsoni and B. vogeli (CB038): smear positivity 7 of 17 complicated vs 6 of 17 uncomplicated, odds ratio 1.28 (0.32 to 5.13). B. canis (CB537): non-overlapping load ranges (23-68% in severe forms vs 2.5-7% in mild), with no group n or test.

Where groups were made by load (the inverse question), damage rose with load: in CB241 (B. canis, 4 vs 4 dogs) 25 of 28 markers were worse in the high-load group (haematocrit g -3.00, -5.02 to -0.98), and in CB187 haemoglobinuria was seen in all high-load dogs and in none of the low-load dogs. Load therefore carries damage between the extremes.

The separate list has 10 items. The strongest are a B. canis vaccination result where clinical disease was prevented with little change in parasitaemia (CB375, review of experimental work), severe haemolytic anaemia with very low smear parasitaemia in 29 B. gibsoni dogs (CB381, abstract only), and the sequestration argument for B. canis that peripheral load understates total load (CB041, review).

sections.heading: What this does not show
paragraphs: It does not show tolerance. With no pooled cell, the literature neither confirms nor rejects that load separates outcome. The 'low load' items are case-level or review statements without a comparison group; they show that discordant cases exist, not how common they are.

Every load here is one moment (mostly at admission), by smear in most units, with the site often not stated. Measurement error in load flattens any slope and can imitate tolerance. Peripheral load may understate sequestered parasites (B. canis).

Load against outcome was reported by only 6 of 42 units with severity rows; studies that measured load and found nothing may not have printed it (selective reporting). Species are never compared: each species has its own sources and definitions. No B. rossi unit reports load against a clinical outcome; the only B. rossi contrast is the experimental dose (CB105), which sets the load by design.
A dog-level test (log load against a health measure, with age and antibody status as modifiers of the slope) needs the author data of part c, a user decision.
